query: Taking nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 as the starting material, what single intervention could prevent its radiation-induced precipitation while retaining its negligible irradiation hardening and improving its suitability for practical bulk fabrication? Formulate one testable hypothesis for energetic-particle irradiation relevant to fusion service, including comparison with the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa; identify the intervention and mechanism, predict quantitative or directional changes in precipitation, irradiation defects, and hardening, define the applicable irradiation and thermal boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and propose a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of high-energy shot peening (HESP) treatment to W38Ta36Cr15V11 will create a gradient nanostructure that annihilates radiation-induced defects, leading to improved radiation resistance and reduced radiation-induced precipitation.
generation.mechanism: Radiation-induced defect annihilation due to gradient nanostructure formation
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved radiation resistance and reduced radiation-induced precipitation
generation.uncertainty: Stability of the gradient nanostructure under irradiation and optimization of HESP treatment parameters

falsification_experiment.design: Irradiation of HESP-treated W38Ta36Cr15V11 at approximately 8 dpa and examination of microstructure and radiation-induced precipitation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HESP-treated W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy shows no significant improvement in radiation resistance and reduction in radiation-induced precipitation compared to the unmodified alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAn equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy was subjected to high-energy shot peening (HESP) to fabricate a gradient nanostructure (GNS) in this work. The microstructures of the GNS samples at different depths within the deformed layer were thoroughly investigated. The microstructure exhibited a transformation from unstressed coarse grains to deformed coarse grains, followed by the formation of ultrafine grains, and ultimately reaching a final nanocrystalline structure with a uniform size of approximately 50 nm. Detailed structural analysis indicated that the deformation process was primarily influenced by the interaction between dislocations and deformation twins, which was attributed to the low stacking fault energy (SFE) of the alloy. The nanocrystalline mechanism was divided into three stages. In the coarse-grained deformation stage, the dislocation band divided twin/matrix lamellae into sub-segments, and the cross twin divided coarse grains into ultrafine grains simultaneously. In this work, the button-shaped ingot of an equiatomic mixture of high-purity (99.97 wt%) Cr, Co, and Ni was melted in a non-consumable vacuum arc melting furnace with a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was flipped and re-melted at least five times, and then homogenization annealing treatment was performed at 1200 °C for 12 h, followed by water quenching. Then, the ingot was cold-rolled with a thickness reduction of 10 to 2 mm (80% reduction). Rectangular-shaped samples of 50 × 20 × 2 mm3 in dimension were cut using electrical discharge machining. Then, the cut pieces were kept at 700 °C for 1 h for recrystallization annealing, and then cooled to room temperature with water. The sample was mechanically polished using silicon carbide abrasive paper until 2000# before the shot peening treatment. cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1.2. The Microstructure of GNSed CrCoNi MEA
cited_evidence.text: Based on the grain size, it can be concluded that the surface gradient nanostructure is composed of four regions: a nanograin layer (0~20 μm), an ultrafine grain layer (20~150 μm), a deformed coarse grain layer (150~250 μm), and an unstressed coarse grain layer (>250 μm).

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4. Irradiation Defects of the MEAs
cited_evidence.text: The irradiated samples did not include any holes or radiation-induced segregation (RIS). Materials exposed to radiation at doses greater than 1 dpa frequently include voids because irradiation-induced vacancies consolidate into stable cavities. Dimensional expansion and a reduction in fracture toughness are two effects of voids. It is believed that radiation-induced segregation, which occurs when alloying elements segregate out of equilibrium near sinks, is a key cause of irradiation-assisted stress corrosion cracking. As a result of the severe lattice distortion in the Three MEAs, irradiation-induced defects may diffuse slowly, inhibiting the growth of defect clusters, and defect annihilation may take place during the transition from amorphization to crystallization under conditions of high atomic-level stress.

decision.rationale: The proposed intervention of high-energy shot peening (HESP) treatment addresses the problem of radiation-induced precipitation in W38Ta36Cr15V11 by potentially creating a gradient nanostructure that can annihilate radiation-induced defects. The mechanism of radiation-induced defect annihilation due to gradient nanostructure formation is physically sound, and the HESP treatment is feasible with established methods.
